Functional Anatomy and Physiology of the Venous System

  • Superficial Veins
  • GSV and SSV
  • They drain the area between the skin and muscle fascia
  • The GSV arises anterior to the medial malleolus
Notes

The Big Picture

Almost everything in this lecture traces back to one mechanism: venous hypertension, specifically a high ambulatory venous pressure. Lymphedema is the parallel story for the second drainage route of the limb, the lymphatics. Use the map to anchor the details that follow.

LECTURE MAP

Chronic venous disease ↑ ambulatory venous pressure Primary = normal deep veins CEAP: C5 healed vs C6 active·Venous ulcer Gaiter area, medial malleolus Pigmentation · LDS · eczema Compression only after ABPI·Investigate non-invasively Venous duplex = first line Reflux > 0.5 s superficial Reflux > 1 s deep veins·Superficial thrombophlebitis Red, tender, palpable cord Duplex: extension to deep? Septic: line out + antibiotics·L I M B D R A I N A G E F A I L U R E Veins & Lymphatics·Varicose vein treatment Compression 30–40 mmHg Sclerotherapy · EVLA · RFA Glue (VenaSeal) · surgery·Lymphedema Painless; foot dorsum involved Positive Stemmer sign CDT → maintenance compression

Each branch is a section of this guide. Gold = the investigation rule that applies everywhere; red = the condition that can turn into DVT.

Notes

Chronic Venous Disease: Pathophysiology

DEFINITION
Chronic venous disease (CVD) is a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations caused by impaired venous function → venous hypertension, particularly elevated ambulatory venous pressure.

Clinical manifestations:

Lower limb pain
Varicose veins
Venous ulcers
Swelling / edema
Skin pigmentation and other skin changes
Complications of varicose veins
  • Pelvic tumour with right-leg DVT two years ago, now pain, swelling and varicose veins → secondary chronic venous insufficiency. 438 ×5
  • GSV might be duplicated
  • There may be accessory veins
  • The SFJ plays an essential part during DVT, SVT and in treatment of varicosities
  • Short Saphenous Vein
  • SPJ is variable
  • Gastrocnemius Veins
  • The gastrocnemius veins arise from the muscle and may join the PV or merge with the SSV
  • 20% incidence of incompetence of the gastrocnemius veins
  • Deep Veins
  • Close to the arteries
  • Duplication exists in most patients
  • Drains 90% of the blood in legs
  • Perforating Veins
    • Link the superficial and deep venous systems
    • Perforating veins are described by anatomic location, such as medial, lateral, posterior, paratibial, and other descriptors
  • Upright body posture demands transportation of blood back to the heart against the force of gravity
    • Arteriovenous coupling
    • Calf muscle pump
    • Competent venous valves
    • Tone of the venous system
    • Suction effect
Notes

Venous Hypertension: Standing vs Walking

Static standing
Gravity → ↑ hydrostatic venous pressure in the foot.
Foot pressure depends on the vertical blood column (height × gravity × blood density).
e.g. a 100 cm column ≈ 100 cm of blood hydrostatic pressure at the foot.
Walking
The calf muscle pump ("peripheral heart") contracts.
Blood is propelled toward the heart.
→ Foot venous pressure falls, provided the valves are competent.

AMBULATORY VENOUS PRESSURE: FROM NORMAL TO DISEASE

NORMAL Walking empties calf veins → foot pressure < 25 mmHg→FAILURE Valve incompetence (reflux) and/or obstruction→RESULT during walking = ↑ AVP → Pressure stays high·CLINICAL Chronic venous insufficiency picture
KEY RULE
Ambulatory venous pressure (AVP) = foot venous pressure measured during walking. Normally below ~25 mmHg (lecture figure). When it stays elevated, the patient develops the clinical picture of chronic venous insufficiency. High AVP is the main cause of venous disease.

Notes

Varicose Veins & Chronic Venous Insufficiency

DEFINITION
Varicose veins = abnormally dilated, elongated, tortuous superficial veins. They are superficial, not deep, veins.
Patients present because of symptoms, cosmetic concerns, or complications; some remain asymptomatic.
CVI and varicose veins are generally progressive, although severity and symptoms may fluctuate.

VV Etiology

Notes

Etiological Classification: Primary vs Secondary

FeaturePrimary varicose veins / CVISecondary varicose veins / CVI
Deep veinsAnatomically and physiologically normalAbnormal: cause venous hypertension via obstruction, reflux, or both
Where the disease isConfined mainly to superficial and/or perforating veinsDeep venous system (± secondary superficial changes)
MechanismIncompetent superficial / perforator valves → reflux → ↑ AVP → varicose veins ± skin complicationsDamaged or blocked deep veins → ↑ AVP
CausesIntrinsic valve incompetence (risk factors: female, age, family history, pregnancies, standing)DVT / post-thrombotic damage · deep venous obstruction incl. iliac vein / IVC thrombosis · previous trauma, major surgery, radiation · AV fistula & vascular malformations · congenital syndromes, e.g. Klippel–Trénaunay
How to tell apartHistory + clinical examination + venous duplex ultrasound
Treatment focusTreat the superficial reflux (compression → sclerotherapy / endovenous / surgery)Manage the underlying deep venous pathology; do not just treat the varicosities
OSCE-IMPORTANT
Primary = normal deep veins. Secondary = abnormal deep veins.

VV Classification

  • The use of CEAP, as reported by the Clinical Practice Guidelines, award a Grade 1A recommendation in the classification of patients with CVD
Notes

CEAP Classification

CEAP = Clinical, Etiological, Anatomical, Pathophysiological classification of chronic venous disease.

C CLINICAL Grades C0 → C6, from no signs to active ulcer·E ETIOLOGICAL Congenital · Primary · Secondary·A ANATOMICAL Superficial · Deep · Perforating (more than one may be involved)·P PATHOPHYSIOLOGICAL Reflux · Obstruction · Both
Notes

C: Clinical Classification

GradeClinical findings
C0No visible or palpable signs of venous disease
C1Telangiectasias (small dilated cutaneous venules: red, pink or blue streaks) or reticular veins
C2Varicose veins
C3Edema due to venous disease
C4Skin / subcutaneous changes: pigmentation, eczema, skin thickening, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche CEAP 2020 subdivides: C4a pigmentation / eczema · C4b lipodermatosclerosis / atrophie blanche · C4c corona phlebectatica
C5Healed venous ulcer
C6Active venous ulcer
• Increasing grade generally means more advanced disease; C5–C6 are the ulcer-related stages.
• Ankle flare (corona phlebectatica): a cluster of small dilated superficial veins around the ankle, associated with chronic venous disease.
EXAM-IMPORTANT
Distinguish C5 = healed ulcer from C6 = active ulcer.
Notes

E, A, P Components

ComponentCategoryMeaning
E: EtiologicalCongenital (Ec)Developmental venous abnormalities / vascular malformations
Primary (Ep)Intrinsic superficial / perforator incompetence without deep venous disease
Secondary (Es)Acquired, identifiable pathology: commonly DVT, trauma, other deep venous abnormalities
A: AnatomicalSuperficial · Deep · PerforatingThe venous system(s) involved; more than one may be affected
P: PathophysiologicalReflux (Pr)Backward venous flow due to valve incompetence
Obstruction (Po)Impaired venous drainage
Combined (Pr,o)Reflux + obstruction

VV Risk Factors

  • Age: >70
  • Gender: Female OR = 2.13
  • Pregnancy and Hormones
  • Positive Family History
    • 90 % when both parents were affected
    • When one parent was affected, the risk is 20 % for M and 62 % for F
    • 20 % risk when both parents were unaffected
  • Genetic Associations
  • Prolonged standing
  • DVT, Thrombophilia and major procedures
  • Others
    • Obesity, smoking, HTN, and decreased physical activity
  • Mother and grandmother had varicose veins; appeared in her 2nd pregnancy → the risk factor keyed → family history. 436 ×3
Notes

Risk Factors for Varicose Veins / CVI

Constitutional Female sex: more common than in males Increasing age: especially the elderly Family history: strong hereditary link; lecturer cited ~90% risk if both parents are affected·Hormonal & lifestyle Multiple pregnancies: hormones + ↑ intra-abdominal pressure Hormonal contraception Prolonged standing: teachers, restaurant workers, barbers, surgeons Obesity / overweight Immobility: poor calf-pump action·Clues to secondary CVI Previous DVT Previous trauma or major surgery Thrombophilia: consider when investigating a patient with previous venous thrombosis
PREGNANCY PATTERN
Varicose veins may worsen during pregnancy and show partial regression / remission after delivery.

VV Clinical Features

  • Progressive disease
  • Remission occurs only after pregnancy and delivery
  • The most frequent complications are
    • Progression to Chronic Venous Insufficiency
    • Skin changes, eczema, skin ulceration, acute bleeding, Superficial thrombophlebitis, infection is less common
  • "When will my varicose veins improve?" → after delivery, if currently pregnant (the only remission). 437

VV Clinical Symptoms

  • Aching, pain, and heaviness
    • Worse on hanging down
    • Relieved on limb elevation and with compression stockings
  • Ankle swelling and tiredness
  • Itching
  • Nocturnal cramps and restless legs
  • Cosmetic disfigurement
Notes

Clinical Presentation of Varicose Veins / CVI

Symptoms

Aching pain, heaviness or discomfort in the legs
Tiredness and fatigue of the legs
Nocturnal leg cramps
Visible dilated, elongated, tortuous superficial veins
Lower limb swelling / edema
Itching (pruritus)
Restless legs
Cosmetic concern: sometimes the only reason to present
PATTERN TO RECOGNISE
Venous pain worsens with prolonged standing and is relieved by leg elevation and compression stockings. Some patients remain asymptomatic despite visible varicose veins.

Chronic venous insufficiency

  • The presence of skin damage (eczema, lipodermatosclerosis)
  • Ambulatory venous hypertension (> 70 mmHg)
  • Failure of the mechanisms lower venous pressure upon ambulation
  • Affects about 10% of the adult population
  • Lifetime risk of chronic venous ulceration is around 1%.
  • Female-to-male ratio is 3:1
  • Aggravated by old age, poor social circumstances, obesity, trauma, immobility, OA, RA, DM and neurological problems
Notes

Signs of Advanced Disease

SignWhat it is
Skin pigmentationBrownish discoloration from chronic venous hypertension
Venous eczemaStasis dermatitis
LipodermatosclerosisChronic inflammatory / fibrotic change of skin and subcutaneous tissue → thickening and induration
Ankle flareProminent small superficial veins around the ankle
Venous ulcerationUsually around the ankle, particularly the medial malleolus
INTERPRETATION
Eczema, pigmentation or lipodermatosclerosis = significant, longstanding ambulatory venous hypertension.

HOW COMMON? (LECTURE FIGURES)

~10% of the population have chronic venous insufficiency·~1% of the population develop venous ulceration·↑ More frequent with age, female sex, obesity, immobility and prolonged standing
Notes

Complications of Varicose Veins

The main reason to treat symptomatic or complicated varicose veins is to relieve symptoms and prevent further complications.

ComplicationMechanism / description
Venous eczema / stasis dermatitisSkin inflammation from chronic venous hypertension
Pigmentation & thickeningChronic venous skin change
LipodermatosclerosisChronic skin / subcutaneous fibrosis
Venous ulcerationSkin breakdown from sustained venous hypertension
BleedingHemorrhage from dilated superficial varicose veins
Superficial thrombophlebitisThrombosis + inflammation of a superficial vein
InfectionInfected venous ulcers → surrounding cellulitis and other infective complications
ProgressionPersistent edema and recurrent ulceration
OSCE-IMPORTANT: COMPLICATIONS TO LIST
Pigmentation · eczema · lipodermatosclerosis · venous ulcer · bleeding · superficial thrombophlebitis · ulcer infection

VV Examination

  • Inspection:
  • Patient should always be standing
  • What am I seeing?
  • Are there any dilated veins over the lower limb?
  • Is it unilateral/bilateral?
  • Which system is involved? GSV/SSV?
  • Which segments are involved? Foot/leg/thigh?
  • Pattern of involvement: truncal/tributary/reticular/telangiectasia
  • Color and size of the veins
Notes

Clinical Examination of Varicose Veins / CVI

General Principles

Always examine the patient standing: varicose veins become more prominent with gravity. Expose both lower limbs adequately, from the thighs to the feet.

1 2 3 4

Examine systematically: inspection then palpation.

Assess the venous disease and any associated arterial pathology.

  • Best position to examine varicose veins → standing. 439 ×3
  • Any limb enlargement with predominantly lateral varices – Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome
  • Is there any swelling?
  • Any skin changes (complications)?
    • SVT, corona phlebectatica, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, and venous ulcers active/healed
  • Scars of previous surgery
  • Are there any dilated veins over the lower abdomen?

Indicates an obstruction to the iliac veins or IVC

Notes

Inspection: What You See → What It Suggests

FindingSuggests
Varicosities on the medial leg / thighGreat saphenous vein (GSV) involvement
Varicosities on the posterior calfSmall saphenous vein (SSV) involvement
Limb swelling (unilateral vs bilateral, severity)Extent of venous disease; consider other causes of swelling
Pigmentation, eczema, thickening / induration, lipodermatosclerosis, atrophie blanche, ankle flareChronic, longstanding venous hypertension
Venous ulcerAdvanced CVI: note location, surrounding skin, ulcer characteristics
Unilateral limb enlargementCongenital venous / vascular malformation, e.g. Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome
Previous surgical scarsPrevious venous surgery or interventions
Dilated superficial abdominal wall veinsCollateral drainage from iliac vein / IVC obstruction or thrombosis → secondary disease
Obviously inflamed, erythematous veinSuperficial thrombophlebitis
  • Palpation
  • Varicose veins are often palpable even when not visible
  • Temperature
  • To identify sites of reflux from deep to superficial veins and also to feel perforators sites
  • Tender induration of acute SVT or the cordlike thickening
  • Ankle joint stiffness
  • Pitting edema and skin turgor
  • Palpation of the Peripheral Pulses
  • Record the Ankle Brachial Index (ABI)
  • Brodie Trendelenburg Test
  • Morrissey’s Cough Impulse Test
  • Multiple Tourniquet Test
Notes

Palpation

Palpate prominent superficial veins and their distribution
Assess lower limb edema
Look for mixed arterial + venous disease, especially if ulcerated

If an ulcer is present:

Check for tenderness / thrombosis: a tender, inflamed, palpable cord = superficial thrombophlebitis
Palpate peripheral arterial pulses for associated PAD
Measure ABPI / ABI when evaluating arterial circulation
Inspect and palpate the ulcer and the surrounding tissue / skin changes.
Check peripheral pulses and regional lymph nodes.

VV Ulcer Examination

  • Inspection
  • Site (location)
  • Number
  • Size
  • Shape
  • Floor - The exposed part of an ulcer ( Inspection)
  • Edges – Part between the margin and the floor of an ulcer (Undermined, Punched out, Sloping, Rolled, Raised)
  • Depth
  • Exudate (Discharge)
  • Surrounding area
  • Margin- Line of demarcation between normal and abnormal
  • Palpation
  • Tenderness
  • Base- the structure on which the ulcer rests (Felt on palpation)
  • Relation with Deeper structures
  • Examination of Surrounding Area
  • Pulses. Scars, nails, hair
  • Examination of Lymph Nodes
Notes

Bedside Venous Tests

Traditional clinical tests of venous incompetence were used in the past but are now less commonly used.

ToolRole
Handheld DopplerBedside assessment of venous flow and possible superficial / deep / perforator valve incompetence
Venous duplex ultrasoundPreferred detailed assessment of superficial and deep venous anatomy and function
EXAM-IMPORTANT: THE EXAMINATION IN ONE LINE
Examine standing → identify which vein is involved → inspect skin and ulcers → palpate arterial pulses → look for evidence of secondary venous disease.
Notes

Venous Ulcer

DEFINITION & PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Venous ulcer = chronic lower limb ulceration caused by sustained venous hypertension, typically from reflux and/or obstruction; it develops in advanced CVI. Several mechanisms of ulcer formation have been proposed, but the lecturer emphasised elevated ambulatory venous pressure as the central cause.
Notes

Location & Clinical Features

Features
Usually superficial; may be painful, especially if infected
Associated: brown pigmentation, skin thickening / induration, lipodermatosclerosis, venous eczema, visible varicose veins, chronic edema
The surrounding skin changes identify the etiology
Classic site: the gaiter area
Lower leg around the ankle, near or above the medial malleolus
High venous pressure here → skin breakdown
Occasionally elsewhere (e.g. the foot), but the medial gaiter region is classic
Notes

Differential Diagnosis of Leg Ulcers

Lower limb ulcers are broadly venous vs non-venous. Differentiate venous ulcers especially from diabetic foot ulcers and arterial ulcers; location and surrounding skin are the major clues.

FeatureVenousArterialDiabetic (neuropathic)
SiteGaiter area, medial malleolusDistal / pressure points: toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shinWeight-bearing areas: plantar metatarsal heads, heel
UlcerShallow, irregular edge, granulating, exudativeDeep, punched-out, pale or necrotic basePunched-out with surrounding callus
Surrounding skinPigmentation, LDS, eczema, edema, varicositiesShiny, hairless, cool, paleCallus; dry skin; reduced sensation
PainMild–moderate; better with elevationSevere; worse on elevation / at nightOften painless (neuropathy)
Pulses / ABPIPresent; ABPI normal (unless mixed)Reduced or absent; low ABPI Arterial and diabetic columns are standard textbook features added for comparison; the lecture focused on the venous column.May be present; ABPI can be falsely high (calcified vessels)
OSCE TRAP
An ulcer in the medial gaiter area near the medial malleolus with pigmentation, skin thickening and varicose veins strongly suggests a VENOUS ULCER. Do not automatically diagnose a diabetic foot ulcer.
Notes

Examining a Venous Ulcer

Document site, size, depth and appearance.

1 2 3 4 5

Inspect edges, base, surrounding skin and evidence of infection.

Assess venous pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, edema and varicosities. Palpate peripheral arterial pulses: is there associated arterial insufficiency? Examine regional lymph nodes where appropriate.

VV Investigations

  • Duplex Scan
  • Reflux in deep veins > 1,000 ms
  • Reflux in other veins > 500 ms
Notes

Investigations of Varicose Veins / CVI

EXAM-IMPORTANT
In vascular surgery, start with NON-INVASIVE tests, especially Doppler and duplex ultrasound. Venous duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice for suspected varicose veins, CVI and venous reflux.

Duplex = anatomical ultrasound imaging combined with Doppler evaluation of blood flow.

  • The most commonly used non-invasive test for acute DVT → duplex ultrasound. 439 ×4
Notes

What Duplex Ultrasound Assesses

ParameterNormalAbnormal
AnatomySuperficial, deep and perforating veins: their course and any structural abnormality
PatencyPatent veinsObstruction / thrombosis, including evidence of DVT
Flow directionUnidirectional, toward the heartReversed / bidirectional = venous reflux
Valve competenceCompetent: no significant backward flowIncompetent: prolonged reflux
Reflux durationBrief = physiological Together these determine whether disease is primary or secondary and guide the treatment plan.Beyond threshold = pathological (see below)

PATHOLOGICAL REFLUX THRESHOLDS (MEMORISE)

> 0.5 s
Superficial veins (> 500 ms)
> 1 s
Deep veins: common femoral, femoral, popliteal (> 1000 ms)

Reflux lasting longer than these thresholds indicates abnormal valve function.

  • Duplex reflux thresholds → > 1 s for deep veins and > 0.5 s for superficial and perforating veins. 438 ×3
Notes

Color Duplex & Pulsed-Wave Doppler

Color Doppler displays flow direction on a color scale. In the lecturer's example, red = backward flow / reflux and blue = heartward flow.
Pulsed-wave (spectral) Doppler produces a waveform showing flow direction and duration. Normal flow is predominantly toward the heart; prolonged reverse flow = valvular incompetence.
Duplex can show both forward flow and reflux in an incompetent GSV or other affected veins.
CAUTION: COLORS ARE NOT FIXED
Red / blue depend on the machine and probe orientation. They show direction relative to the transducer, not universally toward or away from the heart.
  • Venogram
  • CT Venogram
Notes

Additional Investigations

TestWhen / why
CT venography / conventional venographyNot routine for uncomplicated primary varicose veins. Consider when significant iliac vein, IVC or proximal venous pathology is suspected; defines the anatomy and extent of deep venous obstruction.
ABPI / ABIAssesses associated arterial disease, especially before compression therapy in patients with possible PAD.
History, examination and duplex findings together determine the underlying etiology and the treatment.
  • Pelvic tumour resected last year, new varicose veins with saphenous reflux → next CT venogram of the pelvis (look for iliac vein obstruction before treating the superficial veins). 436 ×2

VV Treatment

  • Depends on exam, investigations and preferance
    • Life style modification
    • Compression stockings
    • Cutaneous laser
    • Sclerotherapy
    • Endovenous treatments
    • Surgery

Venous disease — treatment

VV Treatment

  • Depends on exam, investigations and preferance
    • Life style modification
    • Compression stockings
    • Cutaneous laser
    • Sclerotherapy
    • Endovenous treatments
    • Surgery
Notes

Management of Varicose Veins / CVI

Treatment depends on clinical severity, symptoms, complications and venous anatomy. The interventions below mainly concern primary varicose veins with a normal deep venous system.

TREATMENT LADDER: LEAST TO MOST INVASIVE

CONSERVATIVE Lifestyle measures →·CONSERVATIVE Compression therapy→MINIMALLY INVASIVE Sclerotherapy→MINIMALLY INVASIVE Endovenous ablation (thermal / nonthermal)→OPERATIVE Ligation, stripping, phlebectomy
SECONDARY CVI IS DIFFERENT
Manage the underlying deep venous pathology (DVT, deep venous obstruction, AVF, vascular malformations) rather than applying primary varicose-vein treatment indiscriminately.

Lifestyle Modification

  • Exercise
    • Beneficial for ulcer healing
    • Rehabilitate the muscle pump and improve the symptoms of CVI
  • Leg Elevation
    • Elevate their legs 30 cm above the heart several times during the day
  • Weight reduction
  • The avoidance of constricting garments
  • Avoiding Prolonged standing
Notes

A. Lifestyle Modification / Conservative Measures

Regular exercise, especially daily walking: activates the calf muscle pump → better venous return
Avoid prolonged, especially static, standing
Avoid tight, constrictive clothing
Leg elevation: reduces venous hypertension and edema
Weight reduction if overweight / obese
Stay active; avoid prolonged immobility

Goal: reduce venous hypertension, relieve symptoms, and prevent progression.

Notes

B. Compression Therapy

Compression stockings / garments are the major conservative treatment for CVI, edema and venous ulcers. During walking, muscle contraction plus external compression improves venous return and lowers venous hypertension.

KEY NUMBERS & PRINCIPLE
~30–40 mmHg for significant venous edema and ulcer management (lecturer's emphasis).
Graduated: highest pressure at the foot / ankle, decreasing progressively toward the thigh.
Benefits
↓ venous edema / swelling
Relief of aching, heaviness and other symptoms
Improved venous circulation
Promotes venous ulcer healing
Types
Elastic compression stockings
Multilayer compression bandages, especially for venous ulcers
BEFORE STRONG COMPRESSION
Assess for arterial insufficiency first (pulses, ABPI). Strong compression on a limb with significant PAD is dangerous.
  • Reflux at the saphenofemoral junction → stocking length high thigh. 435

Compression Therapy

  • 30 to 40 mm Hg tension results in significant improvement in pain, swelling, skin pigmentation, activity, and well-being
  • Compression therapy is recommended for both patients with venous ulcers, CVI and as an adjunct to venous ablation
  • With a structured regimen of compression therapy, more than 90% of patients with ulcers can achieve complete healing within 6 months
  • 5 days after APR: chest pain, dyspnoea, BP 85/50, HR 120 → CT chest (CT pulmonary angiography). 438 ×12

Wound and Skin Care

  • Controlling bacterial overgrowth with aggressive wound care
  • Treatment with compression stockings with 30 to 40 mm Hg tension
  • Treating varicose veins after complete healing
Notes

C. Management of Venous Ulcer

Compression therapy to reduce venous hypertension and promote healing (after arterial assessment). Appropriate local ulcer / wound care.

1 2 3 4 5 6

Antibiotics if infection is present.

Treat associated edema and surrounding skin disease.

Once healed or controlled: address the underlying venous reflux to reduce recurrence.

In secondary CVI: identify and manage the responsible deep venous condition.

VV Sclerotherapy

  • Venous sclerotherapy is a treatment modality for obliterating reticular veins, and small varicose veins
  • The primary goal of treatment is to target the most proximal source of reflux first and progress to the most distal
Notes

D. Sclerotherapy

MECHANISM
Injection of a sclerosant into an abnormal superficial vein → endothelial injury → eventual venous obliteration.

Mainly used for:

Small superficial veins
Reticular veins
Cosmetic treatment of superficial venous abnormalities
Short-segment varicosities
Telangiectasias

SODIUM TETRADECYL SULFATE (STS): CONCENTRATION FOLLOWS VEIN SIZE

0.25% Very small veins, e.g. telangiectasias→0.5% Intermediate→1% Larger veins

STS was described as the commonly available sclerosant in the lecturer's institution. Rule: smaller vein → lower concentration; larger vein → higher concentration.

VV Endovenous Management

  • Radio-frequency ablation (RFA) and endovenous laser ablation (ELA)
  • Complications
  • Perforation, DVT, PE, phlebitis, hematoma, infection, nerve injury, neovascularization, paresthesia, pigmentation, necrosis, burns, and pain
Notes

E. Endovenous Treatment

Endovenous management = minimally invasive closure / obliteration of incompetent superficial veins from within their lumen. Purpose: eliminate pathological reflux.

TypeOptionsHow it closes the vein
Thermal ablationEndovenous laser ablation (EVLA) Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)Laser / RF catheter or fiber inside the vein delivers controlled heat → thermal injury → closure
Nonthermal ablationSclerotherapyChemical closure
THERMAL ABLATION: PROCEDURECyanoacrylate glue (VenaSeal)Medical adhesive injected inside the vein seals it without thermal energy
1 · ACCESS Ultrasound-guided puncture of the incompetent vein→2 · POSITION Laser fiber or RF catheter introduced into the vein→3 · ABLATE Controlled heat → thermal injury → vein obliterated

Ultrasound guidance is used throughout the procedure.

COMPLICATIONS OF ENDOVENOUS TREATMENT
Uncommon with appropriate technique, precautions and ultrasound guidance.
Skin burns / thermal injury, especially when veins are very superficial
Vein perforation
DVT (rare)

VV Surgical Treatment

  • The primary goal in treating venous insufficiency is to first treat the highest point of reflux
  • Additional goals include eradication of diseased varicosities, minimization of complications, relief of symptoms, and attainment of satisfactory cosmetic results

VV Surgical Management

  • High Ligation of the Great Saphenous Vein
  • Great Saphenous Vein Stripping
    • Stripping of a competent GSV serving as runoff for a varicose collateral vein results in worsening of the collateral varicosity because of resistance to outflow
  • Excision of Local Varicosities (Phlebectomy, Avulsions)
  • Surgery on the Short Saphenous Vein and Veins of the Popliteal Fossa
  • (1) the paucity of studies on significant the role of SSV incompetence to CVI
  • (2) the lower number of SSV reflux than GSV
  • (3) technical considerations
  • (4) the intimate and variable neurovascular relationships of the SSV
  • Indications for Ligation and Stripping of the Great Saphenous Vein in the Current Climate Favoring Endovenous Thermal Ablation

1. treat a superficial tributary of the saphenous vein that is closely adherent to the skin

2. GSV dilatation or aneurysmal venous segments

3. Chronic thrombophlebitis

4. Excessive tortuosity

5. Acute superficial thrombosis

6. Economic consideration

7. Physician choice

Notes

F. Surgical Treatment

Previously the standard treatment; now performed less often because of endovenous techniques.

ProcedureWhat is done
High ligation of the GSVLigation at the saphenofemoral junction, including its tributaries
GSV strippingRemoval of the incompetent GSV with a stripping technique
Multiple phlebectomies / avulsionsRemoval of dilated superficial varicose tributaries through small incisions
High ligation + stripping may be combined with multiple avulsions. Indications for Surgery
IndicationWhy surgery rather than endovenous
Large, aneurysmally dilated superficial veinsToo large for reliable endovenous closure
Very superficial tributaries adherent / close to skinThermal treatment risks skin burns
Chronic / recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis of the varicositiesThrombosed, inflamed segments are removed
Severe tortuosityCatheters / fibers cannot pass
Endovenous equipment unavailableSpecial devices / fibers for EVLA or RFA not available
Patient preference or clinician choiceSelected cases
OSCE-IMPORTANT: PRIMARY VARICOSE VEINS ANSWER
Conservative treatment → compression → sclerotherapy → EVLA / RFA / VenaSeal → surgery (high ligation + stripping ± multiple avulsions), each with its indications.

Superficial venous thrombosis & lymphedema

SVT Risk Factors

  • Trauma or insertion of venous catheters
  • Venous stasis as seen in varicosities
  • Hypercoagulable states
    • factor V Leiden, prothrombin G mutation, protein C and protein S deficiency, antithrombin III abnormalities, and malignant neoplasms
  • OCP, HRT, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged immobilization, recent surgery, trauma, sclerotherapy, history of VTE
Notes

Superficial Venous Thrombosis / Thrombophlebitis

DEFINITION
Superficial thrombophlebitis = thrombosis with inflammation of a superficial vein, in the upper or lower limb. It occurs as a complication of varicose veins or from other provoking conditions.
WHY IT MATTERS
Superficial thrombosis may extend into the deep venous system → DVT.
  • Untreated varicose veins in an obese man — the possible complication keyed → superficial thrombophlebitis. 438 ×2

SVT EPIDEMIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

Involvement of Deep Veins

  • 11% progression to DVT without anticoagulation
  • The most common site of propagation of SVT in the GSV into the common femoral vein
  • Risk factors of presence in non-varicose veins involved, Male, Hx of DVT or PE, age >75 years, inpatient, and CA

SVT Assessment

  • Pain, erythema, tenderness, or induration corresponding
  • Palpable Painful “cords”, and fever or leukocytosis may be present
  • Post- inflammatory hyperpigmentation may occur and last several months
  • Duplex ultrasound scanning has become the initial test of choice for the diagnosis of DVT and evaluation of SVT since
  • D-dimer levels may or may not be elevated in patients

Septic and suppurative Thrombophlebitis

  • Signs and symptoms include pus at the IV site, fever, leukocytosis, and local intense pain
    • Staph aureus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Fusobacterium spp and fungi such as Candida spp
    • Treatment begins with removal of the foreign body and IV antibiotics
    • Excision of the vein is rarely needed to clear the infection

SVT Management

  • LMWH provides the best outcomes with the fewest complications
  • ACCP guidelines for treatment of patients with SVT of the lower limb
    • SVT at least 5 cm in length, use prophylactic dose of fondaparinux or LMWH for 45 days over no anticoagulation
    • Fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily over a prophylactic dose of LMWH is suggested
  • NSAIDs is recommended for upper limb SVT
  • Surgery
    • For SVT within 1 cm of the SFJ
    • Suppurative
  • Topical Therapy
    • Showed reduction in local signs and symptoms, none of these studies evaluated the effect on VTE or SVT extension

  • Anatomy
    • Begins with lymphatic capillaries, which are blind-ended and thin-walled vessels composed of a single layer of lymphatic endothelial cells (LEC)
    • The capillaries then combine to form precollectors and collectors, which connect with LN
    • The collector system is characterized by smooth muscle cells
    • Valves regulate the direction of flow
    • The regional LNs drain fluid from the limbs which then traverses the torso by the cisterna chyli
    • Lymph returns to the blood circulation via the thoracic duct at the junctions of the subclavian and internal jugular veins
Notes

Lymphedema: Basics & Approach

DEFINITION
Lymphedema = accumulation of lymphatic / interstitial fluid due to impaired lymphatic drainage → persistent limb swelling, unilateral or bilateral. Lymphatics are the second route, alongside the veins, for returning interstitial fluid to the circulation.

LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE PATHWAY (LOWER LIMB)

Lymphatic capillaries collect tissue fluid→Larger lymphatic vessels→Lymphatic trunks→Cisterna chyli (abdomen)→Thoracic duct →·Systemic veins at the subclavian junction
Notes

Approach to Limb Swelling

Ask two questions
Unilateral or bilateral?
Acute or chronic?
Then think in four categories
Systemic causes: particularly in bilateral lower limb edema
Venous: venous insufficiency, thrombosis or obstruction
Lymphatic: primary or secondary lymphedema
Infective / inflammatory: including cellulitis

History, examination and appropriate imaging differentiate venous swelling from lymphatic edema.

  • Primary Lymphedema
    • Absence of a known injury and is based clinically on the age of onset
    • Theories: Infection, fibrosis, in uteru dysplasia
  • Congenital
    • present at birth, represents about 15%
  • Praecox
    • Presents during adolescence, represents approximately 75%
  • Tarda
    • Following the age of 35 with about 10% of cases

STEMMER SIGN
Positive Stemmer sign = inability to pinch / lift a skin fold over the dorsum of the base of the second toe, because of tissue thickening and edema. It supports the diagnosis of lymphedema; foot involvement + a positive Stemmer sign help separate lymphatic swelling from other edema.
OSCE-IMPORTANT
Chronic limb swelling involving the dorsum of the foot + thickened skin + positive Stemmer sign → LYMPHEDEMA.

Management of Lymphedema

Conservative, non-surgical management is the mainstay. Aims: reduce limb volume, improve lymphatic drainage, prevent infection and skin complications, and maintain the reduction achieved. Treatment runs in two phases.

Phase 1 · Intensive reduction: Complete / Complex Decongestive Therapy (CDT)Phase 2 · Maintenance
• Manual lymphatic drainage (MLD): specialised massage that moves lymph
• Multilayer compression bandaging: reduces fluid and limb volume
• Exercise therapy: muscle activity drives lymph flow
• Skin care: reduces skin damage and infection risk
• Limb volume monitored during treatment		• Compression garments to hold the volume reduction
• Continued MLD / physiotherapy as appropriate
• Regular exercise and mobility
• Skin hygiene + emollients: prevent dryness, scaling, breakdown, infection
• Prompt treatment of cellulitis / lymphangitis
• Long-term: lymphedema is often chronic
Notes

Surgical Management

Surgery has a limited role compared with conservative therapy, with variable outcomes.

ApproachProcedures
Excisional / debulkingRemoval of extensively edematous / fibrotic skin and subcutaneous tissue; may need skin grafting after extensive excision
Physiological / reconstructiveLymphovenous bypass / anastomosis: redirects lymph into the venous circulation Omental transposition Tissue / lymphatic transfer: lymphatic-bearing tissue moved from another region to improve drainage
preferred first.Success varies between patients and procedures; these are specialised operations, with conservative treatment
OSCE-IMPORTANT
First-line = intensive decongestive therapy (MLD + multilayer compression + exercise + skin care), followed by maintenance compression and physiotherapy. Surgery has a selective role.
  • Goals of surgical treatment
    • Functional, to reduce limb weight and improve skin texture
    • Preventive, to decrease the number of infections and to prevent the occurrence of angiosarcoma
    • Cosmetic, improve the size and shape
  • Surgery should be avoided
    • Patients with minimal edema (<3cm difference in circumference)
    • Gross obesity
    • Actively progressing disease
    • A firm diagnosis of lymphedema is not established
